knowledgeKinds.label: Background
knowledgeKinds.headline: What is it / how does it work
soundsLike: What actually is chronic ankle instability?
Which ligament does what?
What happens to the tissue in the first three weeks?
What is a coper?
knowledgeKinds.pico: Not a PICO question. Population + Phenomenon is enough.
canAnswer: Gives you structure and vocabulary in one pass, which is the actual goal here.
Written to orient, not to answer. That is what you want at this stage.
Where structural claims are actually established.
cannotAnswer: A trial tests an intervention. It cannot tell you what a structure is.
Pooling effect sizes answers nothing about definitions or anatomy.
ladder: Read one textbook chapter or one narrative review. Extract: correct technical terms, 3-5 author names, 2-3 landmark trial names. Do not try to answer anything yet.
Read the IAC selection criteria so you know how the field defines its own population.
redFlags: Reading a 2011 primary study when a 2024 consensus statement exists.
Taking a definition from a course slide rather than from the body that publishes the criteria.
knowledgeKinds.stopRule: Stop when you can write the question down using the field's own vocabulary. That is the entire deliverable of this kind.

knowledgeKinds.label: Intervention
knowledgeKinds.headline: Does X work better than Y
soundsLike: Does balance training reduce recurrence?
Is bracing better than taping?
Should I immobilise this or load it early?
Eccentric or heavy slow resistance?
knowledgeKinds.pico: Full PICO. The Comparator is the part everyone skips and it changes the answer completely.
canAnswer: The only design that isolates the effect of the intervention itself.
Start here, not with individual trials.
Tells you what a panel concluded from the trials — a shortcut, not a substitute.
cannotAnswer: No intervention, no time, no causal claim available.
Confounded by why people chose the treatment they got.
Tells you what changed in the lab, not whether patients did better.
ladder: Read the relevant JOSPT CPG section. It gives you the current consensus position and the vocabulary in one go.
PEDro Advanced Search: subdiscipline musculoskeletal or sports, method systematic review. Then Cochrane, then Epistemonikos. Take the most recent good SR and mine its included-studies table.
Only trials the SR missed or that postdate its SEARCH date (not its publication date — usually 12-24 months earlier). Chase citations forward from the SR.
PROSPERO for reviews in progress, ClinicalTrials.gov for unpublished and negative results.
redFlags: Comparator is nothing. 'Better than no treatment' is close to meaningless in rehab.
Surrogate outcome. Better balance on a force plate is not fewer sprains.
No MCID reported. A statistically significant 2-point change on a 100-point scale is nothing.
Dose not reported. If you cannot reproduce the intervention, the trial is clinically useless to you.
Follow-up under 12 months for a recurrence question.
knowledgeKinds.stopRule: Stop when you have read the most recent high-quality SR plus everything published after its search date, or when new searches only return papers you have already seen.

knowledgeKinds.label: Diagnostic accuracy
knowledgeKinds.headline: Is this test accurate
soundsLike: How good is the anterior drawer test?
Does the Ottawa Ankle Rule rule out fracture?
Can I trust ultrasound for ATFL integrity?
knowledgeKinds.pico: Population + Index test + Reference standard + Target condition. The reference standard is the whole question.
canAnswer: Reports sensitivity, specificity and likelihood ratios against a reference standard.
Pools them, if the reference standards were comparable.
cannotAnswer: Agreement between raters is not accuracy against truth. Two clinicians can agree perfectly and both be wrong.
ladder: Read the ROAST consensus. It tells you which tests the field considers part of a complete assessment at all.
PubMed Clinical Queries, diagnosis category. Look for an accuracy SR first.
Individual accuracy studies. Check the reference standard in each before reading the numbers.
redFlags: No proper reference standard, or the reference standard was applied only to test-positives.
Non-consecutive or case-control sampling — inflates accuracy dramatically.
Reliability reported and presented as if it were accuracy.
Test performed by the person who developed it, in the population it was developed on.
knowledgeKinds.stopRule: Stop when you can state sensitivity, specificity and a likelihood ratio with the reference standard named. Without the reference standard the numbers mean nothing.

knowledgeKinds.label: Prognosis
knowledgeKinds.headline: Who will do badly / how long until return
soundsLike: Who goes on to develop chronic instability?
How long until they play again?
Does a first sprain predict a second?
What predicts a poor outcome?
knowledgeKinds.pico: Population + Prognostic factor + Outcome + Timeframe. No intervention involved.
canAnswer: Follows people forward from a defined starting point. The only honest answer to a 'what happens next' question.
If externally validated. Most are not.
Where consistent effects can be identified.
cannotAnswer: Measures everything at once, so it cannot establish that the factor preceded the outcome.
Its population is filtered by eligibility criteria, so its natural history is not yours.
ladder: Read the IAC 2016 consensus for the base rates — what proportion go on to instability at all.
PubMed with the prognosis filter. Doherty's prospective cohort work is the anchor for first-time sprain.
Individual cohorts. Check follow-up duration and attrition before anything else.
ClinicalTrials.gov and PROSPERO for cohorts still running.
redFlags: Retrospective, presented as if prospective.
Loss to follow-up over 20% with no comparison of completers and dropouts.
Prognostic factor measured after the outcome started developing.
Model developed and tested on the same dataset.
knowledgeKinds.stopRule: Stop when you have a base rate and a confidence interval from a prospective cohort in a population resembling your patient. A point estimate alone is not an answer.

knowledgeKinds.label: Mechanism
knowledgeKinds.headline: Why does this happen, mechanically
soundsLike: Why does the ankle keep giving way?
What changes in gait after a sprain?
Is it the ligament or the nervous system?
What happens to peroneal reaction time?
knowledgeKinds.pico: Population + Phenomenon + Measurement method. There is no intervention and no comparator group in the PICO sense.
canAnswer: Kinematics, kinetics, force plate, motion capture.
Where measurement in vivo is impossible.
cannotAnswer: **This is the most common design mismatch in the whole field.** A trial tells you whether something works, never why.
Guidelines summarise treatment effects, not mechanisms.
ladder: Read the constraints-based model paper (Wikstrom, Hubbard-Turner, McKeon) and Hertel's functional anatomy paper. These two frame the entire mechanism debate.
Tier 1 — by person, not by keyword
**Mechanism literature is found by author.** Open the Scholar profiles of Hertel, Wikstrom, McKeon and Delahunt and sort by citations. This is faster and more complete than any keyword search.
PubMed with the biomechanics filter, plus Connected Papers from one good seed to catch the cluster you missed.
SportRxiv. Biomechanics preprints run well ahead of publication.
redFlags: Causation read into a cross-sectional difference. Almost every mechanism study is cross-sectional.
Lab task chosen for measurability, not relevance. A drop vertical jump is not a sprain mechanism.
Statistically significant kinematic difference of 1-2 degrees, presented as clinically meaningful.
Small n with a large effect — endemic in biomechanics.
knowledgeKinds.stopRule: Stop when you can state the proposed mechanism, the evidence for it, and explicitly which part is inference rather than demonstration.

knowledgeKinds.label: Epidemiology
knowledgeKinds.headline: How common is it
soundsLike: How common are ankle sprains in basketball?
What is the recurrence rate?
Which sport has the highest rate?
What proportion go on to instability?
canAnswer: Systematic capture across a defined population and exposure period.
Where surveillance systems do not exist.
Systematic review with meta-analysis of rates
Doherty 2014 is the anchor for this domain.
cannotAnswer: Its population is selected, so its rates are not population rates.
Captures only those who presented for care — a large undercount for ankle sprain specifically.
ladder: Doherty 2014 Sports Medicine meta-analysis. It is the reference point for incidence and prevalence in this domain.
PubMed with the epidemiology filter, plus the Journal of Athletic Training surveillance literature.
Sport-specific surveillance. Convert every rate to a common denominator before comparing.
redFlags: Denominator not stated, or per-athlete-exposure and per-hour rates compared directly.
Time-loss definition not given, or inconsistent between the studies being compared.
Self-reported injury history over a long recall window.
Military or captive cohorts generalised to recreational sport.
knowledgeKinds.stopRule: Stop when you have a rate with its denominator, its injury definition and its population stated. A bare number is not usable.

knowledgeKinds.label: Qualitative
knowledgeKinds.headline: What does the patient actually experience
soundsLike: Why do patients stop doing their exercises?
What does 'giving way' feel like to them?
Why do people not seek care for a sprain?
What do athletes think 'ready' means?
knowledgeKinds.pico: PEO — Population, Exposure/Experience, Outcome. Not PICO.
canAnswer: The only way to access meaning and reasoning.
cannotAnswer: Measures whether something worked, never why anyone did or did not do it.
A closed-response survey tests your categories, not theirs.
ladder: Search broadly first. This literature is thin in ankle rehab — expect tens of papers, not hundreds.
Look for a qualitative evidence synthesis. If none exists, that is itself a finding worth recording.
Individual interview studies. Read the quotes, not just the themes.
redFlags: Themes presented with no supporting quotes.
No statement of the researchers' own position or how it shaped interpretation.
Sample of convenience presented as if it were purposive.
Counting responses — turning qualitative data into weak quantitative data.
knowledgeKinds.stopRule: Stop when new interviews stop producing new categories in the papers you read. If nothing exists, record 'no qualitative evidence located' — that is a legitimate answer and a genuine gap.

knowledgeKinds.label: Measurement
knowledgeKinds.headline: Is this test or score any good
soundsLike: Is the CAIT reliable?
What is the MCID for the FAAM?
Does the Y Balance Test measure what I think it measures?
Which cut-off should I use?
knowledgeKinds.pico: Instrument + Population + Measurement property. A distinct question type that most routing tables leave out.
canAnswer: Whether a change score means anything.
The proper synthesis for measurement properties.
cannotAnswer: Uses the instrument, does not evaluate it.
Different question — accuracy against a reference standard, not measurement stability.
ladder: Find the original development paper for the instrument. Hiller 2006 for the CAIT.
Search for a COSMIN review of the instrument. Check whether the cut-off has been recalibrated since development.
Individual property studies in the population you care about. Properties do not transfer across populations.
redFlags: Reliability established in a different population from yours and assumed to transfer.
No MCID reported anywhere, yet the score is used to judge change.
Cut-off taken from the development paper when a recalibration exists — the CAIT is exactly this case.
Validity claimed against another unvalidated instrument.
knowledgeKinds.stopRule: Stop when you know the instrument's reliability, its MCID, and the cut-off appropriate to your population — with the source of each.

knowledgeKinds.label: Practice / programming
knowledgeKinds.headline: How do I actually program this on Tuesday
soundsLike: What does week 3 look like?
How many sets, how often, how do I progress it?
When do I let them run?
What are my discharge criteria?
knowledgeKinds.pico: Not answerable by PICO. This is where evidence runs out and structured expert opinion takes over. Be honest about that.
canAnswer: Closest thing to a defensible answer. JOSPT CPGs and the Dutch guideline.
ROAST for assessment, PAASS for return-to-sport decisions.
Often the only place a reproducible dose is written down — read the protocol, not the paper.
Lowest tier. Label it as such when you teach it.
cannotAnswer: Pools heterogeneous doses into an average that describes no actual programme.
Tells you what to target, never how much of it to give.
ladder: JOSPT CPG, then the Dutch 2018 guideline. The KNGF document is 20 years old but its phase structure is still the most directly programmable thing in this domain.
ROAST for what to assess, PAASS and Ankle-GO for return-to-sport criteria.

**Go to ClinicalTrials.gov and read the full protocol** of a trial with the effect you want. Published papers compress the intervention into a paragraph; the registered protocol has the actual sets, reps and progression rules.
Preprints and PROSPERO for what is about to change.
redFlags: Guideline older than 8 years quoted as current — check for a revision every time.
A dose invented to fill a gap and then taught as if it were evidence-based.
Programme copied from a trial whose population is nothing like your patient.
Confusing 'no evidence for' with 'evidence against'.
knowledgeKinds.stopRule: Stop at the current guideline plus one protocol you can actually reproduce. Then write down explicitly which parts of your programme are evidence and which are your judgement.

vocabulary.label: Lateral ankle sprain (the injury event)
vocabulary.why: The index event. Get this wrong and you either drown in every ankle pathology or miss the European literature entirely.
vocabulary.meshNote: "Ankle Injuries" is the workhorse heading but it also indexes fractures and Achilles ruptures. Pair it with a [tiab] concept, never use it alone.
traps: **"supination trauma" is not optional.** Dutch and Belgian groups — which produced the KNGF and Vuurberg guidelines — used this term for years. Omit it and you lose a large slice of the best practical literature.
"ankle injury" without qualification pulls in fractures, syndesmosis injuries and Achilles ruptures. Three different problems, three different timelines.
ATFL is the ligament, not the injury. Searching ATFL alone skews heavily surgical and imaging.

vocabulary.label: Chronic ankle instability
vocabulary.why: There is no MeSH heading for chronic ankle instability. If you search it as a MeSH concept you get nothing. This is the single most common ankle-search failure.
vocabulary.meshNote: NO dedicated MeSH heading exists for CAI. The nearest approximation is "Joint Instability"[mh] AND "Ankle Injuries"[mh] — which is why every good CAI string leans on [tiab] and uses MeSH only as a safety net.
traps: **FAI is a collision.** In this literature it means functional ankle instability. Everywhere else it means femoroacetabular impingement. Never put a bare FAI[tiab] in a string — you will import a hip literature.

"functional" vs "mechanical" instability is a real theoretical split (Hertel's model), not a synonym pair. If your question is about laxity, mechanical is the term; if it is about giving way with normal laxity, functional is.
Papers published before roughly 2014 predate the International Ankle Consortium selection criteria, so their samples may not be comparable to modern ones even when the label matches.

vocabulary.label: Coper (the comparison group)
vocabulary.why: A term you will never guess, and the reason half the CAI literature is comparative. Without it you cannot find the studies that explain why some people recover and some do not.
vocabulary.meshNote: No MeSH heading. [tiab] only. It is a coined research term, not clinical vocabulary.
traps: A coper is someone who sprained their ankle and did **not** go on to develop instability. They are not a healthy control — that distinction is the whole point of the design.
Studies vary on how long post-injury someone must be symptom-free to qualify. Check the definition in every paper.

vocabulary.label: Balance and postural control (the outcome)
vocabulary.why: The MeSH heading is 'Postural Balance', not 'Balance'. Searching the obvious word costs you the indexed literature.
spelling: centre / center of pressure — both spellings appear
vocabulary.meshNote: "Postural Balance"[mh] is the correct heading. There is no "Balance"[mh].
traps: Balance on a force plate is a **surrogate outcome**. Improved sway is not fewer sprains. Do not let a balance-only outcome persuade you an intervention prevents injury.
SEBT and Y Balance Test are related but not interchangeable, and normalisation to leg length varies between studies. Compare raw protocols before pooling results in your head.

vocabulary.label: Proprioception and sensorimotor control
vocabulary.why: Genuine British/American spelling split, plus a cluster of near-synonyms that index differently.
lay: sense of where the joint is
vocabulary.meshNote: MeSH spells it "Kinesthesis" — neither of the two spellings you would type as free text.
traps: Proprioception is measured half a dozen incompatible ways (passive JPS, active repositioning, threshold to detection of passive motion). A null result in one method says little about the others.
"Neuromuscular control" is used loosely and often means the intervention, not the construct. Check which sense a paper intends.

vocabulary.label: Balance / neuromuscular training (the intervention)
vocabulary.why: No MeSH heading exists for balance training. This concept is [tiab] or it is nothing.
spelling: programme (UK) / program (US) — use both, or truncate to program*

vocabulary.label: Ankle dorsiflexion range of motion
vocabulary.why: Several test names refer to the same measurement, and the test name is often the only searchable term.

vocabulary.label: Achilles tendinopathy
vocabulary.why: The correct modern term deliberately excludes decades of literature filed under a term now known to be wrong. You must search the wrong one on purpose.
spelling: tendinopathy / tendonopathy (frequent misspelling in older records)
vocabulary.meshNote: "Tendinopathy"[mh] was introduced relatively recently; older records are indexed under "Tendinitis" concepts. MeSH plus obsolete [tiab] terms is the only complete search.
traps: **Include tendinitis even though it is wrong.** The inflammatory model was abandoned, but twenty-plus years of trials are filed under it. Excluding the obsolete term is the fastest way to build a falsely thin evidence base.
Midportion and insertional are different conditions with different loading responses. Most guidelines cover midportion only — check which one you are reading about.
AT as an abbreviation also means athletic trainer and anterior tibial. Do not use bare AT[tiab].

vocabulary.label: Return to sport
vocabulary.why: The MeSH heading is new. Every paper published before it existed is invisible to a MeSH-only search.

traps: Return to sport, return to participation and return to performance are three different milestones in the Bern consensus framework, not synonyms. A paper reporting one is not answering a question about another.

vocabulary.label: Prevention, bracing and taping
vocabulary.why: Prevention terms split across intervention names and prevention concepts; you need both halves.
spelling: reinjur* catches reinjury and re-injury only if you also write "re-injury" as a phrase
vocabulary.meshNote: "Athletic Tape"[mh] exists and is under-used. Most people search taping[tiab] alone and miss indexed trials.
traps: **Hyphenation kills recall here.** reinjur* does not match "re-injury". Write both.

journals.answers: AOSSM's open-access sibling to AJSM. Surgical and non-surgical sports medicine, free to read.

journals.name: Physical Therapy
journals.note: Hybrid: all articles become free 12 months after publication.
journals.answers: Broad physical therapy science, measurement properties, and profession-level questions. Not ankle-specific but methodologically strong.

journals.name: Journal of Athletic Training
journals.answers: Athletic training research: injury surveillance, epidemiology, and a large share of the chronic ankle instability literature. Fully open access.

journals.name: Physical Therapy in Sport
journals.answers: Clinically applied sports physiotherapy: masterclasses, clinical approaches, and practice-facing research.

journals.name: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
journals.answers: Sports medicine, exercise physiology, biomechanics and motor control. Strong Scandinavian injury-prevention tradition.

journals.name: Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine
journals.answers: Clinician-facing sport medicine: diagnostics, therapeutics and rehabilitation across ages and ability levels.

journals.name: Foot & Ankle International
journals.answers: AOFAS flagship. Foot and ankle reconstruction, trauma and surgical outcomes. The surgical half of your domain.

journals.name: Journal of Foot and Ankle Research
journals.note: MOVED PUBLISHER. Launched 2008 with BioMed Central; now published by Wiley. Older articles still resolve at jfootankleres.biomedcentral.com.
journals.answers: Multidisciplinary foot and ankle: podiatry, orthotics, assessment and management. Fully open access — the most accessible foot/ankle journal you have.

journals.name: Knee Surgery, Sports Traumatology, Arthroscopy
journals.note: MOVED PUBLISHER in 2024. ESSKA's journal is now on Wiley; the Springer archive (link.springer.com/journal/167) remains searchable but no longer receives submissions.
journals.answers: European sports traumatology and arthroscopy. Ankle ligament surgery, osteochondral defects, surgical decision-making.

journals.name: Journal of Biomechanics
journals.answers: Pure mechanics applied to biological problems. Modelling, cadaveric, instrumented. Answers 'why does this happen mechanically'.

journals.name: Clinical Biomechanics
journals.answers: Biomechanics with a clinical question attached. The bridge between a force plate and a patient.

journals.name: Gait & Posture
journals.answers: Locomotion, balance and postural control. Where CAI gait-deviation and postural-control studies live.

journals.name: Journal of Applied Biomechanics
journals.answers: Applied movement biomechanics — sport mechanics, gait and posture, musculoskeletal modelling.

journals.name: Journal of Sport Rehabilitation
journals.answers: Therapeutic exercise, modalities and injury evaluation aimed squarely at rehab practice. A lot of small ankle intervention studies land here.

researchers.name: Jay Hertel
researchers.description: Joe H. Gieck Professor of Sports Medicine and Chair of Kinesiology at UVA, co-director of the Exercise & Sport Injury Lab. Built much of the conceptual scaffolding the CAI field still uses, including the functional-anatomy and pathomechanics model of lateral ankle instability. Works across clinical biomechanics, gait retraining and epidemiology of lower-extremity injury.

papers.title: Functional Anatomy, Pathomechanics, and Pathophysiology of Lateral Ankle Instability

researchers.name: Phillip A. Gribble
researchers.description: Professor and Chair of Athletic Training and Clinical Nutrition at Kentucky, and former Co-Director of the International Ankle Consortium. First author on the Consortium's selection-criteria position statement, which is the document that decides whether a CAI study's sample is comparable to anyone else's. Works on the neuromuscular consequences of ankle and knee injury.

papers.title: Selection Criteria for Patients With Chronic Ankle Instability in Controlled Research: A Position Statement of the International Ankle Consortium

researchers.name: Eamonn Delahunt
researchers.description: Professor in the UCD School of Public Health, Physiotherapy and Sports Science. Lead author of the International Ankle Consortium's ROAST consensus, which defines what a complete clinical assessment of an acute lateral ankle sprain actually contains. Bridges physiotherapy, sports science and biomechanics.

papers.title: Clinical assessment of acute lateral ankle sprain injuries (ROAST): 2019 consensus statement and recommendations of the International Ankle Consortium
The Incidence and Prevalence of Ankle Sprain Injury: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Prospective Epidemiological Studies

researchers.name: Erik A. Wikstrom
researchers.institution: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
researchers.description: Professor of Exercise & Sport Science at UNC. Works on the interaction between musculoskeletal biomechanics and sensorimotor control after ankle injury, with a particular focus on balance coordination. Co-author of the constraints-based model that reframed CAI as a continuum ending in post-traumatic ankle osteoarthritis rather than a static deficit.

papers.title: Understanding and Treating Lateral Ankle Sprains and their Consequences: A Constraints-Based Approach
Epidemiology of Ankle Sprains and Chronic Ankle Instability

researchers.name: Patrick O. McKeon
researchers.description: Professor of Exercise Science and Athletic Training at Ithaca. Research centres on the idea that deficient sensory input from damaged ankle ligament receptors drives the sensorimotor deficits seen in CAI, and on sensory-targeted rehabilitation built from that premise. Read him for the mechanism argument behind balance training.

papers.title: Sensory-Targeted Ankle Rehabilitation Strategies for Chronic Ankle Instability
Understanding and Treating Lateral Ankle Sprains and their Consequences: A Constraints-Based Approach

researchers.name: Claire E. Hiller
researchers.description: Physiotherapist and researcher in the Arthritis and Musculoskeletal Research Group at Sydney, with a PhD in chronic ankle instability and a long clinical background in dance injury. Lead author of the Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool, the patient-reported measure that most CAI inclusion criteria are built on.

papers.title: The Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool: A Report of Validity and Reliability Testing
papers.journal: Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation

researchers.name: Chris M. Bleakley
researchers.description: Professor at Ulster with a focus on acute injury management and early rehabilitation. Work spans cryotherapy, early exercise after ankle sprain, and the question of whether rehabilitation actually reduces reinjury. Co-author on the ROAST consensus.

papers.title: Exercise-based rehabilitation reduces reinjury following acute lateral ankle sprain: A systematic review update with meta-analysis
Clinical assessment of acute lateral ankle sprain injuries (ROAST): 2019 consensus statement and recommendations of the International Ankle Consortium

researchers.name: Cailbhe Doherty
researchers.description: Ad Astra Fellow and Assistant Professor at UCD. His doctoral work was the first prospective analysis of recovery after a first-time lateral ankle sprain, identifying which movement and balance characteristics predict who goes on to develop chronic ankle instability. Also authored the definitive incidence/prevalence meta-analysis.

papers.title: The Incidence and Prevalence of Ankle Sprain Injury: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Prospective Epidemiological Studies

researchers.name: Gino M.M.J. Kerkhoffs
researchers.description: Professor and Chair of Orthopaedic Surgery and Sports Medicine at Amsterdam UMC, founder of the Academic Center for Evidence based Sports medicine (ACES). Works on osteochondral defects and on diagnosis and treatment of ankle injuries. Lead author of the Cochrane review on immobilisation versus functional treatment for acute lateral ligament injury.

papers.title: Immobilisation and functional treatment for acute lateral ankle ligament injuries in adults

researchers.name: Gwendolyn Vuurberg
researchers.description: Radiology resident and postdoctoral researcher trained in Kerkhoffs' group, thesis on the multidimensional management of lateral ankle injuries. First author of the 2018 update of the Dutch evidence-based clinical guideline on ankle sprains, which is the most practically written guideline in this domain.

papers.title: Diagnosis, treatment and prevention of ankle sprains: update of an evidence-based clinical guideline

researchers.name: Evert Verhagen
researchers.description: Human movement scientist and epidemiologist, professor at Amsterdam UMC, director of the Amsterdam Collaboration on Health and Safety in Sports (an IOC research centre) and Editor-in-Chief of BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine. The reference point for whether an injury-prevention programme actually works when implemented, not just in a trial.

researchers.name: Roald Bahr
researchers.institution: Norwegian School of Sport Sciences / Oslo Sports Trauma Research Center
researchers.description: Professor of Sports Medicine and Chair of the Oslo Sports Trauma Research Center, which set the modern template for sports injury surveillance and prevention research. Read him for injury-risk methodology and for how prevention programmes should be evaluated.

researchers.name: Karim M. Khan
researchers.description: Professor of Sports Medicine at UBC and Editor-in-Chief of BJSM from 2008 to 2020, the period in which the journal became the field's centre of gravity. Long-standing work on tendinopathy and on translating evidence into clinical practice.

researchers.name: Karin Gravare Silbernagel
researchers.description: Professor and Associate Chair of Physical Therapy at Delaware, leading the Delaware Tendon Research Group. Thirty years as a physiotherapist and a PhD in Achilles tendinopathy. The primary source on tendon loading protocols and on what return-to-sport looks like for a tendon rather than a ligament.

researchers.name: Kristian Thorborg
researchers.institution: Copenhagen University Hospital Hvidovre / University of Copenhagen
researchers.description: Professor in orthopaedic surgery and sports sciences, based at the Sports Orthopedic Research Center-Copenhagen. Developed validated outcome scores and muscle function tests used worldwide. Most relevant to you for outcome-measure selection and for how return-to-sport testing gets validated.

guidelines.title: Selection Criteria for Patients With Chronic Ankle Instability in Controlled Research: A Position Statement of the International Ankle Consortium
guidelines.summary: Defines who counts as having chronic ankle instability for research purposes: number of previous sprains, frequency of giving-way episodes and feelings of instability, scores on validated self-reported instruments, and severity of the index and most recent injuries. Published simultaneously in JOSPT, the Journal of Athletic Training and BJSM. If you do not know these criteria you cannot read the CAI literature correctly, because a study that ignored them is not describing the same patients as one that followed them.
guidelines.newerVersion: No superseding version found. Operationalised further by the 2019 ROAST assessment statement rather than replaced.

guidelines.title: 2016 consensus statement of the International Ankle Consortium: prevalence, impact and long-term consequences of lateral ankle sprains
guidelines.summary: The Consortium's argument that lateral ankle sprain is not a trivial injury: high recurrence, a large proportion progressing to chronic ankle instability, reduced physical activity and quality of life, and rising rates of post-traumatic ankle osteoarthritis. This is the public-health framing you use to justify treating a first sprain properly. A companion evidence review (PMID 27259753) sets out the underlying data.
guidelines.newerVersion: No superseding consensus statement on this specific question found.

guidelines.title: Clinical assessment of acute lateral ankle sprain injuries (ROAST): 2019 consensus statement and recommendations of the International Ankle Consortium
guidelines.summary: The Rehabilitation-Oriented ASsessmenT. Specifies what a complete clinical assessment of an acute lateral ankle sprain contains — mechanism of injury, bone and ligament assessment, pain, swelling, range of motion, strength, balance and gait — with the explicit purpose of catching the mechanical and sensorimotor impairments that predict chronic ankle instability. BJSM 2018;52(20):1304-1310, DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2017-098885. This is the single most directly usable document in this whole map.
guidelines.newerVersion: None found. Complemented by the PAASS return-to-sport framework (2021).

guidelines.title: Return to sport decisions after an acute lateral ankle sprain injury: introducing the PAASS framework — an international multidisciplinary consensus
guidelines.summary: A three-round Delphi among 155 clinicians working in elite field and court sport, producing 16 consensus items grouped into five domains: Pain severity, Ankle impairments, Athlete perception, Sensorimotor control, and Sport/functional performance. It exists because systematic reviews found no prospectively validated return-to-sport criteria for ankle sprain at all. Treat it as expert opinion with a clear structure, not as validated criteria. BJSM 2021;55(22):1270-1276, DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2021-104087.
guidelines.newerVersion: None found. The Ankle-GO score (2024) is a separate, prospectively tested scoring instrument covering the same decision.

guidelines.title: Development and Validation of the Ankle-GO Score for Discriminating and Predicting Return-to-Sport Outcomes After Lateral Ankle Sprain
guidelines.summary: A composite score combining functional tests and self-reported measures to discriminate and predict return-to-sport outcomes after lateral ankle sprain. A two-year prospective cohort found a low Ankle-GO score at return to sport associated with a large increase in recurrence risk. Included here because it is one of the few return-to-sport instruments in this domain with prospective predictive data behind it rather than consensus alone.

guidelines.title: Ankle Stability and Movement Coordination Impairments: Lateral Ankle Ligament Sprains Revision 2021 — Clinical Practice Guidelines Linked to the ICF
guidelines.body: Academy of Orthopaedic Physical Therapy, APTA (JOSPT)
guidelines.summary: The core rehab guideline for your domain. Covers risk factors, clinical course, diagnosis, examination and intervention for both first-time lateral ankle sprain (under 12 months post-injury) and chronic ankle instability (12 months or more). JOSPT 2021;51(4):CPG1-CPG80. The free PDF hosted by APTA Orthopedics means you never need journal access for this one. Patient-facing summary at jospt.2021.0503 and a practice-change commentary at jospt.2021.0504.
guidelines.newerVersion: Current as of this build; the 2021 edition is itself a revision of the 2013 guideline.

guidelines.title: APTA Orthopedics Clinical Practice Guideline library
guidelines.body: Academy of Orthopaedic Physical Therapy, APTA
guidelines.summary: Entry point to the APTA Orthopedics CPG collection, which hosts free PDFs of the JOSPT ICF-linked guidelines. Included because the JOSPT site itself paywalls most CPGs while APTA Orthopedics often does not. Use this before you try to get institutional access.

guidelines.title: Achilles Pain, Stiffness, and Muscle Power Deficits: Midportion Achilles Tendinopathy Revision 2024 — Clinical Practice Guidelines Linked to the ICF
guidelines.body: Academy of Orthopaedic Physical Therapy, APTA (JOSPT)
guidelines.summary: The current Achilles tendinopathy CPG. JOSPT 2024;54(12). Supersedes the 2018 revision (DOI 10.2519/jospt.2018.0302, PMID 29712543), which is still widely cited and still what most course material quotes. If a course cites the 2018 version as current, that tells you something about the course.
guidelines.newerVersion: This IS the newer version. Explicitly supersedes the 2018 revision.

guidelines.title: Achilles Pain, Stiffness, and Muscle Power Deficits: Midportion Achilles Tendinopathy Revision 2018
guidelines.summary: Martin RL, Chimenti R, Cuddeford T, et al. JOSPT 2018;48(5):A1-A38. Retained here only so you can see what changed between 2018 and the 2024 revision — reading the two side by side is one of the fastest ways to learn what moved in the tendon literature.

guidelines.title: Heel Pain — Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023 — Clinical Practice Guidelines Linked to the ICF
guidelines.body: Academy of Orthopaedic Physical Therapy and American Academy of Sports Physical Therapy, APTA (JOSPT)
guidelines.summary: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, Carreira D, Martin RL, McDonough CM. JOSPT 2023;53(12):CPG1-CPG39. The second update of this guideline. Free PDF via APTA Orthopedics. Note that a 2025 JOSPT commentary reinterprets these recommendations through a non-US lens, which is worth reading alongside it if you practise outside the US.
guidelines.newerVersion: Current. A 2025 international-lens commentary exists (DOI 10.2519/jospt.2025.0202) but does not supersede the guideline.

guidelines.title: Diagnosis, treatment and prevention of ankle sprains: update of an evidence-based clinical guideline
guidelines.body: Dutch multidisciplinary guideline (Vuurberg et al., BJSM)
guidelines.summary: The Dutch multidisciplinary update, BJSM 2018;52(15), DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2017-098106. Practically written and unusually direct: NSAIDs reduce pain and swelling but may suppress healing; supervised exercise-based programmes are preferred over passive modalities for restoring functional joint stability; surgery is reserved for cases that fail comprehensive exercise-based treatment. Often more immediately usable at the treatment-table than the US guidelines.
guidelines.newerVersion: No newer multidisciplinary Dutch update found as of this build.

guidelines.title: KNGF Guideline: Acute Ankle Sprain (English translation)
guidelines.body: Royal Dutch Society for Physical Therapy (KNGF)
guidelines.summary: The KNGF physiotherapy guideline, structured by tissue recovery phase: inflammatory (0-3 days), proliferation (4-10 days), early remodelling (11-21 days), late remodelling and transfer phases. Published as a supplement to the Dutch Journal of Physical Therapy, 2006;116:1-30. A one-page clinical flowchart is available separately. The phase-based structure is the most directly programmable thing in this section — but see the date flag.
guidelines.newerVersion: NOT ESTABLISHED. Two decades old. The Dutch 2018 multidisciplinary guideline (Vuurberg et al.) covers overlapping ground and is far more current. Use the 2018 guideline for recommendations and this one only for its phase structure.

guidelines.title: 2016 Consensus statement on return to sport from the First World Congress in Sports Physical Therapy, Bern
guidelines.body: Consensus group, First World Congress in Sports Physical Therapy (BJSM)
guidelines.summary: Ardern CL, Glasgow P, Schneiders A, et al. BJSM 2016;50:853-864. Not ankle-specific, but it is the document that frames return-to-sport as a shared risk-management decision along a continuum (return to participation, return to sport, return to performance) rather than a binary clearance. Free full-text PDF hosted by IFSPT. Read this before PAASS, because PAASS assumes it.
guidelines.newerVersion: No direct replacement of this specific statement found.

guidelines.title: Immobilisation and functional treatment for acute lateral ankle ligament injuries in adults
guidelines.body: Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (Kerkhoffs GMMJ et al.)
guidelines.summary: The Cochrane comparison of immobilisation against functional treatment for acute lateral ligament injury. Directly relevant to search-string topic 2. Old, and its search date is older still — treat its conclusions as the historical baseline and check what has been published since rather than as the current answer.
guidelines.newerVersion: NOT ESTABLISHED — no updated Cochrane version located from this session. Check the Cochrane Library directly.

guidelines.title: Interventions for preventing ankle ligament injuries
guidelines.body: Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (Handoll HHG et al.)
guidelines.summary: Cochrane review of prevention interventions for ankle ligament injury in physically active people from adolescence to middle age. Relevant to search-string topic 3. Very old; the bracing, taping and neuromuscular-prevention literature has moved substantially since. Use it to see what the question looked like before the modern prevention trials.
guidelines.newerVersion: NOT ESTABLISHED from this session. The prevention evidence base has expanded considerably since 2001.

guidelines.title: Therapeutic ultrasound for acute ankle sprains
guidelines.body: Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (van den Bekerom MPJ et al.)
guidelines.summary: Included mainly as a worked example of a passive modality being formally tested and found wanting. Useful when a patient or a course asks about ultrasound for an acute sprain.

guidelines.title: Cochrane Library — search entry point
guidelines.summary: Search here directly rather than relying on the individual reviews listed above, all of which are old. Cochrane reviews are continuously published and updated as new evidence appears, so the ankle sprain picture may have changed since this map was built.

guidelines.title: What is the quality of clinical practice guidelines for the treatment of acute lateral ankle ligament sprains in adults? A systematic review
guidelines.summary: An appraisal of the ankle sprain guidelines themselves. Read this before you treat any single guideline in this section as authoritative — it tells you which ones were developed rigorously and which were not. Open access.
guidelines.newerVersion: Not checked for a newer appraisal.

guidelines.title: International Ankle Consortium
guidelines.summary: The society that owns this subfield. Its publications page is the authoritative list of position and consensus statements — check it directly rather than trusting any secondary list, including this one. Also runs the International Ankle Symposium.

tools.name: PubMed
tools.purpose: The workhorse bibliographic database. Over 40 million citations from MEDLINE, life science journals and online books, with controlled vocabulary (MeSH), field tags and precise filters.
tools.useWhen: Use it when you need precision and reproducibility — a search string you can save, re-run and email to yourself. Every string in Section 5 runs here.

tools.name: PubMed Central (PMC)
tools.purpose: Free full-text archive of biomedical literature. Where a large fraction of the papers in this map are legally readable in full.
tools.useWhen: Use it when PubMed shows you an abstract and you need the tables. Check here before you email an author.

tools.name: PubMed MeSH Database / NLM MeSH Browser
tools.purpose: The controlled vocabulary used to index MEDLINE. Every indexed paper is tagged with MeSH headings regardless of the words its authors chose.
tools.useWhen: Use it before writing any search string. Look the concept up here rather than guessing the [mh] term — it catches papers that used words you did not think of.

tools.name: PubMed Clinical Queries
tools.purpose: Pre-built, validated search filters for clinical study categories — therapy, diagnosis, prognosis, aetiology — applied on top of your own terms.
tools.useWhen: Use it when you want a design filter you did not have to write yourself, or as a sanity check that your hand-built design filter is not throwing away half the literature.

tools.name: My NCBI — saved searches and email alerts
tools.purpose: Saves a PubMed search and emails you new results daily, weekly or monthly. Set up from the 'Create alert' link under the PubMed search box.
tools.useWhen: Set this up once for each of your core topics and the literature comes to you forever. Highest return on five minutes anywhere in this map.

tools.name: PEDro — Physiotherapy Evidence Database
tools.purpose: Physiotherapy-specific index of RCTs, systematic reviews and practice guidelines. Every indexed RCT carries a PEDro score out of 10 for methodological quality.
tools.useWhen: Use it before PubMed for any 'does this treatment work' question. The pre-scored trials mean you can discard weak studies before reading a word. Physio's structural advantage and most physios never open it.

tools.name: PEDro Advanced Search
tools.purpose: Thirteen fields for defining search terms precisely, including subdiscipline (musculoskeletal, sports) and method (clinical trial, systematic review, practice guideline).
tools.useWhen: Always use this rather than PEDro's simple search. Filter to subdiscipline = musculoskeletal or sports, then sort by score.

tools.name: Cochrane Library
tools.purpose: The highest-rigour evidence syntheses in healthcare, plus CENTRAL, a very large trials register.
tools.useWhen: Use it at Tier 1, before primary studies. If a current Cochrane review exists on your question, its included-studies table is a literature search someone else already did.

tools.name: Epistemonikos
tools.purpose: The largest dedicated database of systematic reviews, with a matrix-of-evidence tool that cross-tabulates every review on a question against every study those reviews included.
tools.useWhen: Fastest way to find ALL systematic reviews on a topic and see instantly which primary studies each one covered. Use the evidence matrix when reviews disagree.

tools.name: Google Scholar
tools.purpose: Broadest coverage including grey literature, theses and preprints. Forward citation chasing via 'Cited by', and author alerts.
tools.useWhen: Use it for chasing, not finding. Click 'Cited by' on a seed paper to get everything published since. Set author alerts on the researchers in Section 2.

tools.name: Semantic Scholar
tools.purpose: AI-backed literature discovery and citation graph from the Allen Institute for AI, with a free API.
tools.useWhen: Use it when you want the citation neighbourhood of a paper without a subscription, or when Google Scholar's ranking is burying what you need.

tools.name: OpenAlex
tools.purpose: Fully open catalogue of 250M+ works, authors, institutions and sources, released CC0. Replaced Microsoft Academic Graph. Now also the home of Unpaywall.
tools.useWhen: Use it for bibliometrics, for building your own tooling on top of a citation graph, or as a free stand-in for Scopus and Web of Science.

tools.name: Unpaywall
tools.purpose: Browser extension that checks a database of millions of legally-deposited open access copies whenever you land on a paywalled article, and shows a green tab if one exists.
tools.useWhen: Install it once. Second step in the access ladder, after your university proxy and before you email the author.

tools.name: PROSPERO
tools.purpose: International prospective register of systematic reviews, run by the Centre for Reviews and Dissemination at York. Nearly half a million registered records.
tools.useWhen: Use it to see what syntheses are being written right now. Tells you an answer is coming 1-2 years before it publishes — and stops you duplicating work.

tools.name: ClinicalTrials.gov
tools.purpose: Registry of clinical trials worldwide, including protocols, planned outcomes and completion status.
tools.useWhen: Use it to find trials in progress, to read a full protocol (dose, progression criteria, outcome timing) that the published paper compressed into a paragraph, and to spot trials that finished but never published — a signal of a negative result.

tools.name: SportRxiv
tools.purpose: Community-led open access preprint server for sport, exercise, performance and health research.
tools.useWhen: Tier 3. Use it to see findings 6-18 months before journal publication. Preprints are not peer reviewed — they generate leads, they do not settle questions.

tools.name: medRxiv
tools.purpose: Preprint server for the health sciences across all disciplines.
tools.useWhen: Same role as SportRxiv but broader. Check both when a topic is moving fast.

tools.name: Trip Medical Database
tools.purpose: Clinical search engine across 75+ sources, ranking results by a publication quality score so Cochrane outranks a journal article which outranks a textbook. PICO search mode built in.
tools.useWhen: Use it for a fast first pass on a clinical question when you want guidelines, syntheses and primary evidence in one ranked list. Free tier is usable; Trip Pro is paid.

tools.name: Connected Papers
tools.purpose: Builds a visual similarity graph from one origin paper using co-citation and bibliographic coupling, so papers that never cite each other can still sit close together. Built on Semantic Scholar data.
tools.useWhen: Paste your seed paper and look for clusters you have not touched. Fastest way to find out you have been reading one corner of a field. Free searches are now capped per month.

tools.name: ResearchRabbit
tools.purpose: Citation-based literature mapping with collections that update as new work appears.
tools.useWhen: Same job as Connected Papers but persistent — build a collection per question and let it keep watching.

tools.name: Elicit
tools.purpose: Automates parts of a literature review: finds papers without exact keyword match, and extracts structured data into a table across many papers at once.
tools.useWhen: Use it to build an extraction table (columns: n, population, dose, comparator, outcome, effect) across the studies you already screened. Verify every extracted cell against the PDF — it is a first pass, not a source.

tools.name: Consensus
tools.purpose: AI academic search over peer-reviewed literature, with a Consensus Meter showing how retrieved papers split on a testable claim.
tools.useWhen: Orientation only, for binary 'does X reduce Y' questions. It tells you where to look. It never terminates a question.

tools.name: scite
tools.purpose: Smart Citations: classifies over a billion citation statements as supporting, contrasting or merely mentioning the cited claim, with the surrounding context shown.
tools.useWhen: Use it before you build any clinical argument on a single study. A paper cited 400 times and contradicted in 30 of them is a different paper than its citation count suggests.

tools.name: NotebookLM (Gemini Notebook)
tools.purpose: Source-grounded AI notebook: upload PDFs and interrogate only that closed corpus, with answers tied to your sources.
tools.useWhen: Feed it the 10-15 PDFs you have already vetted, then ask it to compare doses or find disagreements. The safest AI use in this entire workflow, because the corpus is one you chose. Recently renamed Gemini Notebook by Google.

tools.name: PEDro scale
tools.purpose: The 11-item scale used to rate every RCT indexed in PEDro. Based on the Delphi list developed by Verhagen and colleagues at Maastricht. A free online training programme exists.
tools.useWhen: Applies to RCTs. Rough heuristic: 6 or above is worth your reading time, 4 or below is close to noise. Check blinding, intention-to-treat and dropout yourself rather than trusting the total.

tools.name: Cochrane RoB 2
tools.purpose: The revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomised trials, released 2019. Five domains: randomisation process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, outcome measurement, and selection of the reported result.
tools.useWhen: Applies to RCTs, and it is what Cochrane reviews use. More rigorous and slower than the PEDro scale — use RoB 2 when a single trial is going to change what you do.

tools.name: AMSTAR 2
tools.purpose: Sixteen-item critical appraisal tool for systematic reviews of healthcare interventions, seven of them designated critical. Produces an overall confidence rating: high, moderate, low, or critically low. The instrument is contained in the open-access 2017 BMJ paper.
tools.useWhen: Applies to systematic reviews. Was it registered on PROSPERO? Two independent screeners? Is the search date stated? Those three questions alone filter most of the field.

tools.name: ROBIS
tools.purpose: Risk-of-bias tool for systematic reviews (not for the primary studies inside them), covering interventions, diagnosis, prognosis and aetiology reviews. Three phases; four domains in phase 2.
tools.useWhen: Use alongside or instead of AMSTAR 2 when you are appraising reviews for an overview. Cochrane and JBI both accept either.

tools.name: QUADAS-2
tools.purpose: Quality assessment of diagnostic accuracy studies. Four domains: patient selection, index test, reference standard, and flow and timing.
tools.useWhen: Applies to 'is this test accurate' questions. The two that matter most: was there a proper reference standard, and were patients consecutive rather than cherry-picked? NOTE: QUADAS-3 has now been released and is the current recommended version.

tools.name: QUIPS
tools.purpose: Quality In Prognosis Studies. Six bias domains: study participation, study attrition, prognostic factor measurement, outcome measurement, study confounding, and statistical analysis and reporting. Hayden JA et al., Ann Intern Med 2013;158:280-286.
tools.useWhen: Applies to 'who will do badly' and 'how long until return to sport' questions. Attrition is usually where prognosis studies fall over.

tools.name: GRADE Handbook
tools.purpose: The framework for rating overall certainty of evidence across a body of studies as high, moderate, low or very low, and for grading strength of recommendation.
tools.useWhen: Use it when you are summarising a whole body of evidence rather than one study — which is what your written note in Section 8 of the research system actually is.

tools.name: CASP Checklists
tools.purpose: Free critical appraisal checklists from the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme, one per study design — RCT, systematic review, cohort, case-control, diagnostic, qualitative, economic.
tools.useWhen: Use these when you are learning to appraise, or for designs where you do not have a specialised tool. Plain language and quick.

tools.name: CONSORT 2010
tools.purpose: Twenty-five-item reporting checklist plus participant flow diagram for randomised parallel-group trials. Linked here to the open-access PLOS Medicine version of the statement.
tools.useWhen: Use it in reverse: if a trial does not report an item CONSORT requires, ask why. Missing dose detail or a missing flow diagram is a red flag, not an oversight.

tools.name: PRISMA 2020
tools.purpose: Reporting guideline for systematic reviews and meta-analyses, updated in 2020 from the 2009 version.
tools.useWhen: Use it to check whether a review reported its search date, databases, screening process and exclusions. A review that will not tell you its search date cannot be assessed for currency.

tools.name: STROBE
tools.purpose: Reporting guideline for observational studies: cohort, case-control and cross-sectional.
tools.useWhen: Applies to epidemiology and prognosis papers. Check whether the study was genuinely prospective and how loss to follow-up was handled.

tools.name: EQUATOR Network
tools.purpose: Central searchable library of over 500 reporting guidelines across every study design, with checklists and flow diagrams.
tools.useWhen: Use it when you hit a design you do not have a checklist for. Search by study type.

checklist.text: Create a My NCBI account and save search string 1 with a weekly email alert
Save the remaining 9 search strings to My NCBI (weekly or monthly)
Set Google Scholar author alerts for Hertel, Gribble, Delahunt, Wikstrom, McKeon
Set Google Scholar author alerts for Hiller, Bleakley, Doherty, Silbernagel
Set a Google Scholar 'Cited by' alert on the ROAST 2019 consensus statement
Set journal TOC alerts: BJSM, JOSPT, Sports Medicine, Physical Therapy in Sport, JFAR
Download the free JOSPT Lateral Ankle Ligament Sprains 2021 CPG PDF and read it once, properly
Read the IAC selection criteria (2014) and ROAST (2019) — these two define the field's vocabulary
Create a PEDro bookmark straight to the Advanced Search page, not the homepage
Check PROSPERO and ClinicalTrials.gov for your subfield — set a quarterly reminder
Set up the question-note template (Q / ANSWER / CONFIDENCE / EVIDENCE / CONTESTED / UNKNOWN / CLINICAL RULE / SEARCH STRINGS THAT WORKED)
